H1.text: A library sorts its books by subject. A music scale repeats after eight notes. A shopkeeper keeps an empty shelf for stock that is still coming.

H2.text: Sorting, repeating, and leaving a gap. The periodic table was built on all three ideas.

H3.text: Aarav sees the problem tonight. His notes on the elements are a pile of loose pages, in no order.

H4.text: Chemists in the eighteen hundreds had the same mess, only much bigger.

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will see how one chemist described elements that nobody had found yet.

P1.text: So why classify elements at all?

P2.text: In eighteen hundred, only thirty one elements were known. By eighteen sixty five, sixty three.

P3.text: Today we know one hundred and eighteen. Learning each one alone is almost impossible.

P4.text: So we sort them into families. Elements in one family behave alike.

P5.text: Learn one member, and you already know a lot about the rest of its family.

U1.text: Three big attempts led to the table. Dobereiner in eighteen twenty nine. Newlands in eighteen sixty five. And Mendeleev in eighteen sixty nine.

S1.text: Let's test each idea on our molecule bench. First, Dobereiner's triads. A triad is a group of three.

S2.text: Calcium, strontium and barium behave alike. Their atomic weights are forty, eighty eight, and one hundred thirty seven.

S3.text: Add the first and the last. Forty plus one thirty seven is one seventy seven. Half of that is eighty eight point five.

S4.text: And strontium, the middle one, weighs eighty eight. The middle weight is close to the average of the other two.

S5.text: But only a few triads worked. So the idea was dropped as a coincidence.

S6.text: Next, Newlands. He lined up the elements in order of atomic weight.

S7.text: Lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine. Then the eighth is sodium.

S8.text: And sodium behaves like lithium. Every eighth element is like the first, just like eight notes on a music scale.

S9.text: He called it the law of octaves. It worked only up to calcium. After that, the pattern broke.

M1.text: Then came Mendeleev. He also ordered the elements by atomic weight, but he grouped them by how they behave.

M2.text: His periodic law. The properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights. Periodic means repeating at regular steps.

M3.text: He trusted properties over weights. Iodine is a little lighter than tellurium.

M4.text: But iodine behaves like chlorine and bromine. So he put iodine after tellurium, in their group.

M5.text: And where no known element fitted, he left a gap. A gap below aluminium, and a gap below silicon.

M6.text: He even described the missing elements. He called them eka aluminium and eka silicon. Eka is Sanskrit for one: one place below.

M7.text: Look at his guess for eka aluminium, next to gallium, found in eighteen seventy five.

M8.text: Atomic weight, sixty eight guessed, seventy found. Density, five point nine guessed, five point nine four found.

M9.text: Oxide, E two O three guessed. Gallium forms G a two O three. Almost a perfect match.

B1.text: Now eka silicon. It sits right below silicon, and silicon's oxide is S i O two.

B2.text: Pause and think. Which oxide should eka silicon form? E O two, or E two O three?

B3.text: E O two! Elements in one group combine in the same way. Germanium, found in eighteen eighty six, forms G e O two.

T1.text: Remember this. A good classification does not just sort. It predicts.

W2.text: Chlorine, bromine and iodine form a triad. Their atomic weights are thirty five point five, eighty, and one hundred twenty seven.

W4.text: Step one. Add the first and the last. Thirty five point five plus one twenty seven is one sixty two point five.

W5.text: Step two. Take half. One sixty two point five divided by two is eighty one point two five.

W6.text: Step three. Compare. Bromine weighs eighty. That is very close to eighty one point two five.

W7.text: So yes. Bromine sits in the middle, just as the triad rule says.

X2.text: Many students write that Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic number.

X3.text: He did not. Mendeleev used atomic weights. Atomic number came later, from Moseley, in nineteen thirteen.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As one mark recall questions. Triads, octaves, and which real elements filled Mendeleev's gaps.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which statement about early classification is correct? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Mendeleev's eka aluminium was later found as gallium.

A2.text: A is wrong. The law of octaves worked only up to calcium.

A3.text: B is wrong. Mendeleev used atomic weights, not atomic numbers.

A4.text: D is wrong. In a triad, the middle weight is close to the average of the other two, not their sum.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Calcium is forty and barium is one thirty seven. What weight does the triad rule give strontium?

Y3.text: Two. Why did Newlands' law of octaves fail after calcium?

Y4.text: Three. Why did Mendeleev place iodine after tellurium?

N1.text: Next time: if atomic weight is not the true key, what is? We find out in the modern periodic law.
